127.title: This one counts
127.hook: Epictetus: when you kiss your child, remember they are mortal (Discourses 3.24)
127.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism sometimes follow Epictetus's advice from the Discourses and the Handbook: in a moment of affection, they quietly remember that the one they love is mortal, and let it deepen their attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: premeditatio, Seneca's rehearsal after a city burned. Your line was foreseen is lighter.

It's bedtime. You lean over a sleeping child, or a partner, or an old dog curled on the rug, and for a second, out of nowhere, a thought arrives that you'd rather not have. One day, this won't be here. Most of us flinch and push it away, as if thinking it might make it happen. Nearly two thousand years ago, Epictetus told his students something that shocked some of them. Don't push it away. Let it come, right in the middle of the tenderest moment.
screen: `LEANING OVER A SLEEPING CHILD.` → `ONE DAY, THIS WON'T BE HERE.` → `DON'T PUSH IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: In the Discourses, book three, Epictetus says, in paraphrase: when you kiss your child, what harm is there in whispering, tomorrow you may die? A student objects: that's ill-omened. You'll bring bad luck. Epictetus answers: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested? Or that leaves fall in autumn? It's simply naming something that belongs to nature. There's nothing unlucky in the truth. In the Handbook he's briefer: when you kiss your child, remember you are kissing a human being, a mortal, so that if they die, you won't be shattered. That's his own reason, and it's worth being honest about it: steadiness, loving what you have without pretending you'll have it forever. Some readers find that cold. But many people who try the practice find something else inside it. The thought doesn't make them love less. It makes the moment sharper. You don't take the goodnight for granted. You look a little longer. You say the thing you were going to say tomorrow. That's the whole week, really. Marcus rose above the city and saw everyone at once. Voyager showed one speck. The astronauts looked back. Memento mori, remember you will die. Seneca rehearsed the loss so it couldn't ambush him. And Epictetus brings it all the way home, to one face, one hug, one ordinary evening. Not someday. This one counts.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, a person or an animal, and picture their face. Let the true thought come, gently, they are mortal, and so am I, and notice what it does to how you see them. Then picture the next time you'll greet them, and how you'd like to hold that moment.
Epictetus. The Stoic who told his students to remember, even while kissing someone they love, that they are mortal. Today's word.
Your line: look a little longer. Not someday; this goodnight. Day one hundred twenty-seven, done.

128.title: Five remembrances
128.hook: the Buddha's five: I will age, fall ill, die, be parted from what I love, and my actions are my own (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57)
128.howItsDone: In some Buddhist communities, including Theravada monasteries and Plum Village practice centers, the five remembrances are recited aloud as part of a chanting session.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus, who said to remember, even while you kiss someone you love, that they are mortal. Your line was look a little longer.

Here's a list nobody pins to the fridge. Not the dentist appointment, but the big ones underneath: getting old, getting sick, the people you'll one day lose. That list usually stays folded. Yet one teacher asked people, women and men, householders and monks alike, to take it out and read it. Often. Slowly. Not to frighten themselves, but because, he said, it loosens something. This week has kept endings in view: the view from above, memento mori, Seneca's rehearsal, the hug that counts. The Buddha closes it with his list.
screen: `THE LIST WE DON'T OPEN.` → `READ IT OFTEN.` → `THE FIVE REMEMBRANCES.`

segments.voice: It comes from a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of the Buddha's numbered discourses, book of fives, number fifty-seven. In plain words: One: I will grow old; I can't escape aging. Two: I will fall ill; I can't escape illness. Three: I will die; I can't escape death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. Five: my actions are my own. I am their owner and their heir; whatever I do, good or harmful, that is what I will inherit. The surprise is who it's for. The text says women and men, householders and monks, should reflect on these often. Not just the monastery. Everyone. And it gives reasons. Remembering age softens the pride of youth. Illness, the pride of health. Death, the pride of simply being alive. Remembering parting loosens the grip of craving. Then the fifth turns everything around. The first four are about what will happen to you. The fifth is about what you do. Age, illness, death and parting are not up to you. That may echo the line Epictetus drew earlier this month, though the two come from different worlds and mean different things. In the Buddha's list, the one thing you truly own is your conduct. So the list doesn't end in gloom. It ends in your hands. You can't stop the clock. You can choose what you say at dinner tonight.

segments.voice: Say each one inside, with a whole breath before the next: I will grow old; I will fall ill; I will die; I will be parted from what I love; my actions are my own. If one of them stings, let it, and soften the shoulders. Then stay with the fifth, and let it point at one thing you'll do today.
Five remembrances. Four things that will happen to everyone, and one thing that belongs to you: what you do. Today's word.

129.title: Solved by walking
129.hook: a Latin saying, later attached to Diogenes: it is solved by walking
129.howItsDone: Writers, philosophers and plenty of others take a walk to think a problem through, and the Latin phrase solvitur ambulando is sometimes quoted to describe it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five remembrances, ending with the one thing you own. Your line was my actions are my own.

An hour on the same problem, and nothing. The email you can't word. The decision about the job, the move, the conversation. You've made lists. You've asked three friends. Your head feels like a room with the windows shut. Then you give up, go out to buy milk, and somewhere around the second corner the answer just arrives, as if it was waiting for your legs. People have noticed this long enough to give it a Latin name. A new week starts today: walking, the body, and sleep.
screen: `STUCK FOR AN HOUR.` → `A WALK FOR MILK.` → `THE ANSWER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Solvitur ambulando means it is solved by walking. The story it's attached to is older than the phrase. In ancient Greece, the philosopher Zeno of Elea built famous puzzles meant to show that motion is impossible: to cross a room, you must first cross half of it, and half of that half, forever, so how do you ever arrive? The story goes that when someone argued this to Diogenes the Cynic, he didn't answer. He stood up and walked around. Diogenes Laertius, a biographer writing long afterward, tells a version of it. The Latin tag came much later again, and people have pinned it on Diogenes ever since, though Diogenes spoke Greek, so the words were never his. But the idea caught on, and grew. Some philosophers took long walks to think. Nietzsche wrote that only thoughts that come from walking have any value. Modern science has poked at it too. In a 2014 Stanford study, people came up with more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, even walking on a treadmill facing a blank wall. It was a lab task, not a life decision, so it's a clue, not a promise. Still, notice what walking does. It moves the body, so the mind loosens its grip. It gives your eyes something new every few steps. And it sets a gentle rhythm, left, right, that your thoughts can ride on. Sometimes you don't solve it. You walk it.
screen: `IT IS SOLVED BY WALKING.` · `DIOGENES STANDS UP AND WALKS.` · `A LATIN TAG, ADDED LATER.` · `THE 2014 STANFORD WALKERS.` · then, large: `WALK IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Let one question come up, something real you've been chewing on, and say it once, clearly, inside. Then set it down, the way you'd put a bag on the floor, and feel your feet. Picture a ten-minute walk later, the question riding along but not driving, and for now just breathe with it nearby.
Solvitur ambulando. Latin for it is solved by walking, a saying pinned on Diogenes, who answered an argument by getting up and moving. Today's word.

130.title: Walking meditation
130.hook: slow walking, feeling each step, as taught in Buddhist monasteries
130.howItsDone: In Buddhist monasteries of several schools, monks and visitors alternate sitting meditation with walking meditation on a short straight path, walking slowly and turning at each end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diogenes stood up and walked, and the Latin said it is solved by walking. Your line was walk it out.

Early morning, a monastery courtyard in Thailand or Myanmar. A monk walks a straight path of maybe twenty paces. At the end, he stops, turns slowly, and walks back. Then again. And again. For an hour. He isn't going anywhere, and that's the point. Most walking is getting from here to there: to the car, to the fridge, to the next thing, with the mind already arrived. This kind has nowhere to arrive. Every step is the whole trip. Yesterday's walk was for thinking. Today's is for not thinking.
screen: `A MONK ON A SHORT PATH.` → `TURN, AND WALK BACK.` → `NOWHERE TO ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: In the Pali texts, the word for it is cankama, walking up and down, and the walking path itself carries the same name. In one short teaching from the book of fives, the Buddha lists five benefits of walking meditation. It gives you endurance for journeys. It gives you endurance for effort. It's good for health. It helps digestion. And the calm you find while walking lasts a long time. That last one matters: a calm that can walk is a calm you can take into the day. The practice looks different from school to school. In Burmese vipassana, taught by teachers like Mahasi Sayadaw, you break each step into parts and note them silently: lifting, moving, placing. In Zen, kinhin is walking meditation between long sits, slow, hands held at the chest, one half step to each breath. In the twentieth century, the Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught walking meditation to large groups, often outdoors, in Asia, Europe and North America. The common thread is simple. Feel the foot. Feel the weight shift. Let the next step be the only step. When your mind drifts to the grocery list, and it will, you notice, and come back to the sole of your foot. It's the same move as watching the breath, done with legs.
screen: `CANKAMA: WALKING UP AND DOWN.` · `FIVE BENEFITS OF WALKING.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `FEEL THE FOOT, COME BACK.` · then, large: `THIS STEP.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can; if not, keep your feet on the floor where you sit. Shift your weight into one foot, then lift, move and place the other, feeling the heel, then the whole sole, take the weight, and say inside: this step. Take ten steps slower than feels normal, and if you run out of room, turn slowly and come back.
Walking meditation. Slow steps on a short path, feeling each one, as taught in Buddhist monasteries. Today's word.
Your line: this step. Every step is the whole trip. One hundred thirty days now.

131.title: Thoreau's sauntering
131.hook: in his essay Walking (1862), Thoreau praises going out with no destination
131.howItsDone: Some readers of Thoreau take aimless walks in his spirit, without a route or a goal, and his essay Walking is still read by hikers and nature writers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: walking meditation, a short path, slow steps, turn and come back. Your line was this step.

When did you last go out with no errand? Not to the store, not to hit a step count, not walking the dog on its schedule. Just out the door, turning left because left looked nice. If the answer takes a while to find, that's an answer too. A man in Concord, Massachusetts, spent hours a day doing exactly that, and treated it as serious work. He wrote an essay about it, printed in the year he died.
screen: `NO ERRAND, NO STEP COUNT.` → `CONCORD, MASSACHUSETTS.` → `THOREAU'S SAUNTERING.`

segments.voice: Henry David Thoreau wrote Walden, about his life in a cabin by a pond. But his essay Walking, published in the Atlantic in 1862, just after his death, has a lighter step. It opens boldly: "I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness." He says he's met only one or two people in his life who understood the art of walking, people "who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering." Then he plays with where the word saunter comes from. One story, he says, is that it comes from wanderers in the Middle Ages who asked for charity on their way, they claimed, to the Holy Land, la Sainte Terre. So a saunterer is a Holy-Lander, and every walk can be a small pilgrimage. Another story he offers: sans terre, without land or home, and so at home everywhere. The honest part: modern dictionaries say nobody really knows where saunter comes from, and Thoreau's stories read more like poetry than history. But look at what he's doing with them. A walk without a destination isn't lazy. It's a kind of pilgrimage, where the holy land is wherever your feet happen to be. He claimed he needed four hours a day of it to stay well in body and spirit. You don't need four hours. You need one walk where nothing is the goal.
screen: `WALKING, 1862.` · `A GENIUS FOR SAUNTERING.` · `HOLY-LANDER, OR WITHOUT LAND.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE ROOT.` · then, large: `SAUNTER.`

segments.voice: Picture your front door, then picture stepping out and turning whichever way looks inviting: no errand, no route, no timer except a rough sense of when to head home. Notice what that feels like in your body, freedom or a little itch to be useful. Both are fine.
Thoreau's sauntering. Walking with no destination, which he treated as a small pilgrimage with the holy land wherever you are. Today's word.
Your line: saunter. The holy land is wherever your own two feet are. Until tomorrow.

132.title: The body scan
132.hook: moving attention from feet to head, central to Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR course (1979), drawn from Buddhist practice
132.howItsDone: In Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction courses, participants practice a guided body scan, usually lying down for about forty-five minutes, moving attention slowly through the body from the feet to the head.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Thoreau and the art of going nowhere in particular. Your line was saunter.

Quick question: how are your feet right now? You probably had to go and check. That's normal. Most of the day it's easy to live about six inches behind the eyes, with the rest of the body just carrying the head around. It only gets attention when it hurts. In 1979, in a hospital in Worcester, Massachusetts, a scientist named Jon Kabat-Zinn started a course for patients with chronic pain and illness that doctors had run out of ways to help. One of the first things he taught them was to lie down and visit their own bodies, one part at a time, starting at the toes.
screen: `HOW ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A HOSPITAL, 1979.` → `THE BODY SCAN.`

segments.voice: The course was called Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, MBSR for short, begun at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center. It's eight weeks long, and the body scan sits right at the start. You lie on your back and move your attention slowly: the toes of the left foot, the sole, the heel, the ankle, up the leg, then the right, the hips, the belly, the back, the hands, the arms, the shoulders, the neck, the face, the top of the head. At each place you simply notice. Warm, cold, tingling, aching, nothing at all. Nothing at all counts too. You're not trying to relax, though that often happens. You're trying to be there. Kabat-Zinn was open about where he learned this: from Buddhist meditation, which he practiced for years before shaping it for a hospital. The roots go deep. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha's great teaching on mindfulness, one exercise is to review this very body from the soles of the feet up, and from the crown of the head down. The word in Pali is kayagatasati, mindfulness of the body. MBSR set the religious framing aside so anyone could use it, and it's been studied a great deal since, with real but moderate benefits for stress. You spend all day living in your body. The scan is a way of showing up there on purpose, and saying, part by part: here I am.
screen: `MBSR: EIGHT WEEKS, 1979.` · `TOES TO THE TOP OF THE HEAD.` · `NOT RELAXING: BEING THERE.` · `ROOTS IN BUDDHIST PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Sitting or lying down, start at your feet and ask what's there, warmth, pressure or nothing, then move up through the legs, the belly rising and falling, the back, the hands, the shoulders, the jaw, the eyes and the top of the head. Don't fix anything; just visit. At the end, feel the whole body at once, and say inside: here I am.
Kayagatasati. The old Pali name for mindfulness of the body, attention moving slowly from the feet to the head, noticing without fixing. Today's word.
Your line: here I am. Your body is where you live all day. Day one hundred thirty-two, done.

133.title: Where you hold it
133.hook: stress often lands in the jaw, shoulders or belly
133.howItsDone: Some people use progressive muscle relaxation, tensing and then releasing each muscle group in turn, and relaxation courses often teach a quick check of the jaw, shoulders and belly during the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kayagatasati, feet to head, noticing without fixing. Your line was here I am.

Where are your shoulders right now? Don't change anything first. Are they sitting low and easy, or have they crept up toward your ears? Your teeth: touching, or pressed together? Your belly: soft, or pulled in like you're bracing for a hit? Often at least one of them turns out to be on duty, holding something, for no reason anyone could name. That's what yesterday's scan was quietly turning up. Today gets specific.
screen: `SHOULDERS BY YOUR EARS?` → `TEETH PRESSED TOGETHER?` → `WHERE YOU HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: When the body senses a threat, it gets ready. In a 1915 book, the American physiologist Walter Cannon described that readiness for fighting or for flight, and fight or flight is the name that stuck. The heart speeds up, breathing quickens, and muscles tighten, ready to strike or run. That's useful if there's a bear. The trouble is that a hard email, a traffic jam or a tense dinner can set off a smaller version of the same thing, with nothing to strike and nowhere to run. So the tension just stays, and it tends to settle in the same few places. The jaw: some people clench their teeth when stressed, often without knowing, some even in their sleep. The shoulders: they rise and round forward, a little like a turtle pulling in. The belly: the muscles brace, and breathing moves up into the chest. In 1929, a Chicago doctor named Edmund Jacobson published a book called Progressive Relaxation. His discovery was simple: people often can't feel how tense a muscle is until they first tighten it on purpose, and then let go. The contrast teaches the body what soft feels like. None of this needs a teacher or a mat, just a habit of checking. These three places are where a hard day tends to show, and you can let them go, one muscle at a time.
screen: `FIGHT OR FLIGHT, 1915.` · `THE BEAR THAT ISN'T THERE.` · `JAW, SHOULDERS, BELLY.` · `TIGHTEN, THEN LET GO.` · then, large: `LET THE SHOULDERS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Let your teeth part a little, lips closed, tongue resting. Lift your shoulders toward your ears on purpose, hold for a breath, let them fall and feel the difference, then once more. Last, let the belly go soft and the breath drop down into it, and each time something tightens, notice, and let it down again.
Jacobson. The doctor who found that tensing a muscle on purpose, then letting go, teaches the body what soft feels like. Today's word.
Your line: let the shoulders down. Soft is something the body can learn. Rest easy; see you tomorrow.
